body: Gray comes up in the one window over Theo’s desk, and down in the Anacapa lot the sodium lights go out a pole at a time, as if someone is walking the row with a very large thumb. At the far end, under the last pole to go, Kevin’s mother’s Odyssey sits with the dew on its windshield taking the first of the light. Over Jack’s desk Rosie’s crayon princes come up out of the gray, crowns first.

body.text: Her Candlemas candle stands unlit in the Steubenville mug on Jack’s desk, the wax set white down one side.
body.else: His own Candlemas candle, the one he is saving for Nonna, stands unlit in the Steubenville mug on his desk.

body: He is up first, in yesterday’s clothes with the pillow’s seam still printed down one cheek, at Theo’s MacBook, because Jack has never owned a laptop and his Marisol mail lives in a second window on Theo’s. Behind him the blanket on Theo’s bed has not moved since midnight. Two new messages. The first, in bold, is from Priya Raman, RA, 4th floor: *REMINDER: QUIET HOURS ARE NOT SUGGESTIONS.* Attachment: *laminated_copy.pdf.* The second is Hale’s, sent to all twelve of them at 11:40 last night, ten minutes before Jack said yes to anybody.

body.title: PHIL 109H — Thursday
body.text: Thursday’s seminar will not meet. I shall be in Berkeley, the city, giving a lecture to people who have paid to disagree with me. The dog remains in Marisol with Mr. Marsh. For Monday, everyone: Percy, *The Moviegoer*. Those of you who will be in Louisiana may read it there and write to me about its accuracy. —A.H.

body: *Berkeley, the city*, to tell it apart from Bishop Berkeley, the dog, who stays; Jack can hear the clause in Hale’s vowels, tucked in at the corners like a hospital bed. And then *those of you.* Hale has twelve students and no information, which has never slowed him down. Jack hasn’t asked him for the week yet. Office hours are nine to ten and the man flies at eleven, so the asking will have to be done at a trot.

Across the room the RAZR begins to buzz its way sideways along Jack’s desk toward the mug, and the outside screen lights with a 504 number he doesn’t know. Behind him Theo’s breathing, which for hours has been the breathing of a sleeping man, becomes the breathing of a man imitating one. The blanket climbs to cover the other ear.
Jack gets there before the mug does and flips it open. “Hello?”
“*Bonjour, le garçon de l’Ohio.* You know who this is.”

body.text: He is standing in his socks on the cold floor, at very nearly attention, in the posture of a fourth-grader at St. Brigid’s being asked the Commandments in order. He knows the voice. He has heard it twice, both times through Lena’s phone: on the speaker in the Fishbowl kitchen in November, informing him he was skinny, and for ten seconds over break, asking was he eating.
body.else: He is standing in his socks on the cold floor, at very nearly attention, in the posture of a fourth-grader at St. Brigid’s being asked the Commandments in order. He knows the voice. He has heard it once, through Lena’s phone over break, for ten seconds, asking was he eating.

body: “Yes, ma’am.”
“Nine o’clock here, and you sound like you’re still in the bed.”
“It’s seven here, ma’am.”
“Seven.” A lid goes down onto a pot, thoughtfully, in Louisiana. “*Bon.* Seven’s not early. By seven I’ve won my first argument.” Then: “You remember what I told you.”
“Come to this house first.”

“*Bon.*” Behind her something is being chopped on a board, steadily, by a person with a grievance, and an AM radio is discussing the Saints at length and in several accents. “*La rousse* gave me this number. The redhead. She calls Celeste every night now. I don’t know what for. Celeste says she’s *organized*.”

Jack holds the RAZR out and looks at it. Laney Price has handed him a *Jack* with nothing on it, at civil intervals, for a month. It appears she has also been working the long-distance lines to Dupre Street. “Yes, ma’am,” he says to the 504 number.

“Wednesday you said no. I do not ask why; a person’s why is his own. Wednesday night you said yes. I do not ask that either. The redhead told Celeste, and Celeste told me before her coffee.” It is accurate to the hour. Somewhere between the Pacific and the Gulf there is a wire, and he has been on it all week. The chopping stops. “So you have said yes to the rich boy, and I am calling anyway. You don’t come because the rich boy asked you. You come because I asked you.”
“Yes, ma’am. I’ll —”
“Don’t bring nothing.”
“Ma’am, I can’t show up at somebody’s house with —”
“You bring something, Celeste has to find a place to put it. You bring yourself. You eat. You go to Mass with us Sunday. You eat shrimp?”
“I eat what’s on the table, ma’am.”
“That is the right answer.” A spoon rings off a rim. “We will see if it is the true one. Thirty hours, Celeste says. In a Honda.”
“It’s a minivan, ma’am. It’s a very good one.”

“In my day we drove to Lafayette and it was a vacation.” Jack has never seen that kitchen and could draw it: the onions going clear in the iron pot, the cayenne tin, a stove that was old when Tony was a boy. The chopping starts again, harder. “Tony has been sick to his stomach since the Vikings. Since *January.* I told him, Tony, it is a game, and he looked at me like I said something about his mother. Sunday I do not care who wins. I care who is at my table.” The board goes quiet. “I told Magdalena I was calling you. She said, *Mémère, don’t.*” The spoon taps the rim twice. “So.”
Which settles whose invitation it is, and he has had worse news from better sources. On Dupre Street a pot is waiting, and he has about a second and a half.

journal.title: Odile Broussard (Mémère)
journal.text: Lena’s Mémère. Breaux Bridge. Eighty-eight. The monks’ fruitcake came; it’s *trop sec*; she’s eating it anyway. Prayed for Wes at the eight o’clock. *Quelqu’un devait demander.* Asked for le garçon de l’Ohio. Wes told her I’m skinny. I said oui, madame. She says I have manners. The Friday before I flew back she took the phone for ten seconds to ask was I eating. When I come to New Orleans I come to her house first. Thursday at seven in the morning she called me herself, from Dupre Street, on a number the redhead gave her. She knew I’d said yes. She called anyway: I don’t come because the rich boy asked me, I come because she asked me. Don’t bring nothing. Come to this house first — I said it back to her. Lena told her not to call.

choices.text: “I’ll come to your house first, ma’am.”
choices.key: Mémère called you herself at seven in the morning. You told her you’d come to her house first.
response: “I know you will. I’m the one who said it.” Then, away from the phone and at three times the volume, in French: not the big pot, the other one, and who has touched her roux. A lid rings down. The line is a kitchen for a moment, and then it is nothing at all, and Jack is left with “Thank you, ma’am, I’ll —” in his mouth and no one to put it to.
“Who was that?” Theo asks, from under the blanket.
“Oh, *really*,” says the blanket, and goes to sleep at once, which is to say unconvincingly: it begins to snore, in the wrong key. On the nightstand Hollis, in his teacup, keeps his own counsel.

choices.text: “I’ll bring my appetite, ma’am. That’s not bringing something.”
choices.key: Mémère called you herself at seven in the morning and told you not to bring anything. You said you’d bring your appetite. She allowed it.
response: “That’s the only thing you’re allowed.” Something comes down the line that is not quite a laugh, short and dry, a screen door on a spring. Then she is shouting at someone in the yard, in French, about a chicken, and the screen door slaps for real, and the call is the sound of Dupre Street in the morning, and then not even that.
Theo is up on one elbow, hair in every direction, like a man who has never slept in his life. “Who was that?”
“Oh, *really*,” Theo says, and lies back down, and is asleep before he has finished the word, with one eye not entirely shut.

choices.key: Mémère called you herself at seven in the morning. You told her you’d already said yes. Now you’d said it to her.
response: “I know. Now you said it to me.” Far back in the house, a voice that must be Celeste’s asks who is on the phone, and Mémère, without covering anything, says, “*Le garçon,*” the way you’d name a delivery. “Thank you, ma’am, I’ll see —” Jack says, and Celeste says something else, and the line goes to the kitchen and then to nothing.
“Who was that?” Theo asks, to the ceiling. He has not moved.
“Oh, *really*.” Theo’s breath evens out into sleep so promptly that a stranger could have heard it was fake from the hall.
